block.text:
Up until this point, we have written programs that were using the tester library to print the fields of objects. Now, we are going to learn how to write stand-alone programs that do not depend on the tester library. The key method that enables us to write such stand-alone Java programs is the main() method.

In Java (and in many other programming languages), the main() method is where your program begins execution. In other words, when you run a stand-alone Java program, the main() method is the first method to get executed. A class with a main() method in Java looks like the following:

To run this program we use two commands, javac and java. Assuming we stored this in a file called HasAMainMethod.java, running the program would look like this (where we use $ as an abbreviation for whatever your terminal prints before you type the command):

$ javac HasAMainMethod.java 
$ java HasAMainMethod
$

Do Now! Click "Run", and you should see a terminal. Type these two commands into the terminal (and press enter after each one). Observe what happens (or if anything even happens!) after each one.

At the moment, this program does.... nothing! It doesn't even display any text to let us know whether we've succeeded or failed.

Actually, it would give some kinds of feedback if we caused errors. For example, if we delete a curly brace and re-run with the same terminal commands, the javac command will report an error:

Do Now! Run the javac HasAMainMethod.java command and then java HasAMainMethod. When running them in that order, which command, javac or java, first caused an error?
